doc.title: Will Shade and Dewey Corley Interview, 1960-05-25

title: Starting Roosevelt Sykes on piano; working sawmills not farms
summary: Corley says he showed Roosevelt Sykes his first piano sketches in Arkansas, played little blues himself, and worked sawmills and quarter boats instead of farming.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: I'll tell you who I do know of. Who's that? Roosevelt Sax. I know him too. I started him off on piano doing call in hell long song. Is that right? I play a little piano myself, not very much blues, but I'm his background, like some room is my background in the drug band.
Oh, I see. You started him off. That's
In hell in Arkansas. His first record record was the 44. I wore my 44 so long until it made my shoulder sore. Yeah.
I didn't teach him how to sing. I just showed him little sketches on the piano as I know. It wasn't very much that I know.
Well, what did you sing out there? What kind of numbers did they have out there in !
Oh, just just ordnett blues that's all just ordnett blues what I should say.
Do you remember the names or the lyrics to any of them?
Well, I don't because I wasn't very much in music at all. See, I don't know songs or nothing like that.
What were you doing at the time? Chopping cotton or something?
Well, I didn't much see no ! I used to work at sawmill and things work on quarter boats and things all
time. I never farmed never was farming.
Well, that's good. It's hard work.

That's right. And hard. And hard work too. Yeah. I tell you. And it's too much ups in farming. You got to first wake up. Next thing you if you don't get no money at the end of the fall you be missed. Yeah.
That's right. Yeah. Well, it's too much ups to the work. It's too much ups in farming. Too much down to the prices too.
